recipes.title: Trinxat
recipes.summary: Andorra's mountain dish — mashed cabbage and potato fried into a crisp cake with garlic and bacon.

steps.text: Boil the cabbage and potatoes together in salted water until very soft. Drain thoroughly.
Fry the garlic and bacon in the oil until crisp. Lift out half the bacon for garnish.
Add the cabbage and potatoes to the pan and mash roughly with a spatula, mixing in the garlic and bacon fat.
Press into a cake and fry until a golden crust forms underneath, then flip and brown the other side.
Serve topped with the reserved bacon.

recipes.title: Luqaimat
recipes.summary: Crisp-shelled, fluffy fried dough balls scented with cardamom and saffron, drizzled with date syrup and sesame.

steps.text: Whisk the batter ingredients into a thick, smooth, sticky batter.
Cover and leave in a warm place until doubled and bubbly.
Heat the oil to 170 °C. Squeeze small balls of batter through your fist and scoop them off with a wet teaspoon into the oil (or use two spoons).
Fry, turning, until deep golden all over (4–5 minutes). Drain on paper.
Drizzle with date syrup and sprinkle with sesame. Serve warm.

recipes.title: Kabuli Palaw
recipes.summary: Afghanistan's national dish — lamb buried in spiced basmati rice, crowned with sweet caramelised carrots, raisins and nuts.
equipment: Heavy ovenproof pot with a lid

items.prep: on the bone, in large pieces
items.name: lamb shoulder

steps.text: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear, then soak it.
Fry the onions in the oil until deep brown — this colours the dish. Add the lamb and brown it all over.
Add the water and salt and simmer, covered, until the lamb is tender.
Lift out the lamb. Measure 750 ml of the broth (top up with water if needed) and stir in the spices.
Meanwhile fry the carrots in 3 tablespoons of oil from the pot until soft, add the sugar and raisins and cook until the raisins plump. Toast the nuts in the same pan. Heat the oven to 160 °C.
Parboil the drained rice in salted boiling water for 4 minutes and drain. Put it in the pot with the spiced broth, nestle in the lamb, and cook uncovered over medium heat until the broth is absorbed.
Cover tightly and bake (the "dam" stage) until the rice is fluffy and separate.
Pile the rice on a platter with the lamb, and top with the carrots, raisins and nuts.

recipes.serving: On a large shared platter with salad and yogurt.

recipes.title: Fungee and Pepperpot
recipes.summary: Antigua's national dish — a thick vegetable and meat stew with greens, eggplant, squash and okra, served with fungee, a firm cornmeal and okra mash.

steps.text: Simmer the beef and salt pork with the water, onion, garlic, thyme and Scotch bonnet until tender.
Add the vegetables and simmer, stirring, until they break down into a thick stew. Remove the pepper and season.

For the fungee, boil the okra in the salted water until soft, then stir in the soaked cornmeal and keep turning with a wooden spoon over low heat until stiff and smooth (about 15 minutes). Stir in the butter and shape in a buttered bowl.
Serve the fungee turned out beside the pepperpot.

recipes.title: Baked Lamb and Yogurt
recipes.summary: Baked lamb and yogurt (tavë kosi), is an Albanian recipe.

steps.text: Cut meat into 4 serving pieces, and sprinkle each piece with salt and pepper. Bake in a moderately-heated oven with half the butter, basting the meat with its gravy now and then.
When meat is half-baked, add rice. Remove the baking pan from the oven and leave it aside while you prepare the yogurt sauce.

Sauté flour in butter until mixed thoroughly. Mix yogurt with salt, pepper and eggs until a uniform mixture is obtained, and finally stir in the flour-butter mix. Put the sauce mixture in the baking pan; stir it with the meat pieces.
Bake at 375°F (190°C) for about 45 minutes. Serve hot.

recipes.title: Tavë Kosi
recipes.summary: Albania's national dish — tender lamb baked under a thick, tangy yogurt and egg custard until golden.

steps.text: Season the lamb with salt and oregano. Brown it in the butter in an ovenproof dish, add the water, cover and roast at 180 °C until tender (about 60 minutes). Stir in the rice for the last 20 minutes, if using.
Melt the butter, stir in the flour and cook 1 minute. Cool slightly.
Whisk the yogurt and eggs together, then whisk in the butter-flour mixture, nutmeg and salt.
Pour the yogurt over the lamb.
Bake uncovered at 200 °C until set and golden on top.

recipes.title: Spas
recipes.summary: A soothing soup of tangy yogurt and hulled wheat, stabilised with egg and finished with butter-fried onion and dried mint.

steps.text: Simmer the barley in the water until tender.
Whisk the yogurt, egg, flour and salt until smooth in a pot.
Heat the yogurt mixture over medium heat, stirring constantly in one direction, until it comes to a simmer — the egg and flour stop it curdling.
Add the barley with its water and simmer 5 minutes.
Fry the onion in the butter until golden, add the mint off the heat, and pour over the soup. Add the herbs.

recipes.serving: Hot in winter or chilled in summer.

recipes.title: Muamba de Galinha
recipes.summary: Chicken stewed in red palm oil with okra, squash, tomato and garlic — Angola's national dish, eaten with funge.

steps.text: Season the chicken with lemon juice, garlic and salt and marinate.
Heat the palm oil over medium heat (don't let it smoke). Brown the chicken, then add the onions and cook until soft.
Add the tomatoes, chili and water, cover and simmer.
Add the squash and okra and simmer until the chicken and vegetables are tender and the sauce has thickened.

recipes.serving: With funge (a stiff cassava- or corn-flour porridge) and beans.

recipes.title: Chimichurri
recipes.summary: A sharp, herby sauce of parsley, oregano, garlic, chili, vinegar and oil — the essential partner to Argentine grilled meat.

items.note: or a mix of olive and sunflower oil
items.name: olive oil

steps.text: Dissolve the salt in the hot water to make a brine (salmuera).
Combine the parsley, oregano, garlic and chili in a jar. Add the brine and vinegar, then the oil.
Leave at room temperature to let the flavours mingle.

tips: It improves over a day in the fridge and keeps for about a week.
recipes.serving: Spooned over asado (grilled beef), choripán (sausage sandwich) or grilled vegetables.

recipes.title: Austrian Napkin Dumpling
recipes.summary: Serviettenknödel (ˌsɛr.vi.ˈɛt.ɛn ˈknø:dɘl) is a type of knoedel, a bread dumpling that plays an integral role in the culinary traditions of Austria, Bavaria, and the Czech Republic.

steps.text: Mix the milk, eggs and salt together. Combine the mixture with the bread cubes and the parsley in a large mixing bowl, coating as much of the bread as possible with the mixture. Let the mixture rest.
Chop and sauté the onions. Cool enough to not cook the eggs, add them to the bread mixture, and mix thoroughly.

Let the mixture rest for an hour, mixing it through once or twice during the hour. The object here is to coat the cubes with the liquid mixture on all sides to allow them to absorb as much liquid as possible; this is especially necessary if your bread is more than a few days old.

Wet a fresh cotton dishcloth, tea towel, or cloth napkin. Some cooks brush the top side of the cloth with melted butter for more flavor, but this is not necessary. Completely unfold the dishcloth and place the bread mass in the middle of the cloth.

Next, form the bread mass into a 3-inch (~6 cm) thick log. Roll bread log up tightly in the cloth and tie off the ends of cloth with a short length of string or twine. Some cooks also tie a string around the middle as the edge of the cloth tends to pucker in the middle.
Bring a large pot of water to a boil, and then add salt. Slowly lower the serviettenknödel into the water and let cook for 40 minutes.
Remove the serviettenknödel from the boiling water with tongs (or two forks in a pinch) and transfer to a large cutting board. Cut and remove the string; then unroll and remove the cloth.
To prepare the knödel for the table, begin at one end and cut ½-inch (1 cm) slices, taking only as many as you need in servings so that the knödel does not get cold.

tips: The amount of butter can also be lessened or substituted with a neutral-tasting oil.
A wooden cutting board is preferred, as the wood will absorb much of the excess water in the cloth.

recipes.title: Holzknechtnocken
recipes.summary: Holzknechtnocken, translated as Lumberjacks’ Dumplings, is a traditional dish from Ebensee in Austria. In former times lumberjacks had to stay in the forest for days and would prepare dumplings.

steps.text: Mix flour and salt in a large bowl and add water. Knead until you get a dough.
Form dumplings and add them to a pot of boiling water. When dumplings rise to the surface of the water, they are done.
Melt lard in a heavy-bottomed skillet with deep sides. Add dumplings, and fry until they are golden.
Serve with sauerkraut or steamed apples.

recipes.title: Kasnocken
recipes.summary: Kasnocken are small dumplings combined with melted cheese. In Germany, "Nocken" are called "Spaetzle". They have their origins in Schwaben, a region in Southern Germany, and are served as a side dish to roasts.

steps.text: Mix flour, eggs, water, and salt carefully to get a dough; it should neither be stiff nor too soft.
Pass the dough through a special press for dumplings into boiling, salted water.
Boil the small dumplings for about 3 minutes, then drain and rinse them with cold water.
Melt the butter in a pan, add the dumplings, and season them with salt and pepper.
Gradually add the grated cheese and stir vigorously.
When all of the cheese has melted, heat butter in another pan, add the onion rings, and fry them until they become golden brown.
Top the dumplings with the onion rings and chives.

recipes.title: Pastries Filled with Jam
recipes.summary: Marmeladetascherl are a variety of sweet filled pastry originating in Austria.

steps.text: Mix the flour with the baking powder, and rub in the butter. Then, add the curd and the salt, and knead it into dough.
Let the dough rest in the fridge for 1 hour.
Roll the dough to about 2 mm thick, and cut it into 10 cm squares.
Put a blob of jam in the middle of each square, and fold them diagonally. Press the edges to seal the tascherl.
Brush a bit of the egg white onto each tascherl, and place onto a baking sheet.
Preheat the oven to 180°C, put the tascherl into the oven, and bake them for approximately 20 minutes.
Before serving, dust some sugar onto the tascherl to add some extra flavour.

recipes.title: Wiener Schnitzel
recipes.summary: Thin veal cutlets in a puffy, golden breadcrumb coat, fried in plenty of fat and served with lemon.

items.note: about 140 g each, from the leg
items.name: veal cutlet

items.prep: beaten with 1 tbsp milk or cream
items.name: egg

items.note: or clarified butter or vegetable oil
items.name: lard

steps.text: Place each cutlet between sheets of plastic wrap and pound evenly to about 4 mm thick. Season with salt.
Dredge in flour, dip in the egg, then lay in the breadcrumbs and coat lightly without pressing (pressing stops the crust puffing).
Heat the fat in a large frying pan to about 170 °C — it should be at least 1.5 cm deep.
Fry the schnitzels one or two at a time, swirling the pan so hot fat washes over the top, until the crust puffs and turns golden (2–3 minutes per side).
Drain on paper and serve immediately with lemon.

recipes.serving: With Viennese potato salad or parsley potatoes and lingonberry jam.
recipes.culture: In Austria, "Wiener Schnitzel" must by law be made with veal; pork versions are called "Schnitzel Wiener Art".

recipes.title: Anzac Biscuits
recipes.summary: Chewy-crisp oat and coconut biscuits sweetened with golden syrup, baked for Anzac Day.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 160 °C and line two trays with baking paper.
Mix the oats, flour, sugar and coconut in a bowl.
Melt the butter and golden syrup together. Dissolve the soda in the boiling water and stir it into the butter — it will foam.
Pour the foaming mixture into the dry ingredients and mix well.
Roll tablespoons of the mixture into balls and place on the trays, well spaced. Flatten slightly.
Bake until golden. They firm up as they cool — bake longer for crisp, less for chewy.

recipes.culture: Associated with the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps of World War I; the name "Anzac" is protected by law in both countries.

recipes.title: Damper
recipes.summary: Damper is Australian bushman's bread, made while camping or "waltzing matilda" (carrying a swag around looking for work). It is meant to be made outside by a campfire.

steps.text: Add salt to flour.
Add water, then mix and form into a round loaf.
Dig a 1 foot-deep hole near a fire, and fill it with 2 shovels of hot coals and ash.
Add damper mixture to a greased camp oven (traditional cast iron round pot with lid).
Cook in the hole for a maximum of 40 minutes. If undercooked it will be flat and rubbery.
Your first try may be inedible. Keep trying, you'll soon be an expert.

tips: This cookbook also has a Drover's damper recipe.
You can do this in a barbecue grill with the mixture in greased metal foil as well. During cooking, damper increases in volume by ⅓ to ½, so allow room for expansion.
If you aren't outdoors, just add mixture to greased oven tray and bake in a moderate oven for 30–40 minutes.

recipes.title: Drover's Damper
recipes.summary: Drover's damper is Australian bread, made by stockmen while taking care of or rounding up stock. It is meant to be made outside by a campfire. This is the "flash" version, made when butter and milk are available.

steps.text: Add salt to flour, then add sugar.
Rub in butter.
Mix in milk to make a medium-soft dough.
Knead lightly on flat surface until smooth.
Pat dough into a round shape.
Place damper mixture on coals or hot ash. Cook for maximum of 40 minutes.
Discard burnt outside and eat the inside.
Serve with butter, (golden syrup) or jam.

tips: This cookbook also has an "ordinary" damper recipe.
You can do this using a hole near the fire in a greased camp oven or greased aluminium foil in a barbecue.
If you aren't outdoors, just add mixture to greased bread tin, brush with milk and cook in a hot oven, reducing heat until cooked (20 minutes).
You can add dried fruit to make "Johnny Cake".
As a variation, add grated cheese.
Use beer instead of milk to make "Beer Damper".

recipes.title: Qutab
recipes.summary: Paper-thin half-moon flatbreads stuffed with a mountain of fresh herbs and greens, cooked on a dry griddle and brushed with butter.
equipment: Large dry frying pan or saj

steps.text: Knead the dough ingredients until smooth, cover and rest for 30 minutes.
Mix the greens with the salt, squeeze lightly, and drain off excess liquid. Add the sumac.
Divide the dough into 12 balls and roll each into a very thin 18 cm circle.
Spread a thin layer of filling over half of each circle, fold over and press the edges to seal.
Cook on a hot dry pan for 1–2 minutes per side until speckled brown. Brush generously with butter and stack.

recipes.serving: With yogurt and an extra sprinkle of sumac.

recipes.title: Ćevapi
recipes.summary: Little grilled sausages of seasoned minced beef and lamb, stuffed into fluffy somun bread with raw onion, kajmak and ajvar.

steps.text: Knead the meats with the garlic, soda, salt, pepper and water for 5 minutes until sticky. Cover and chill overnight.
With wet hands, shape into fingers about 2 cm thick and 7 cm long.
Grill over hot coals or on a griddle, turning, until browned and just cooked through (8–10 minutes).
Warm the bread on the grill, split it, and fill with 5–10 ćevapi, onion and kajmak.

recipes.serving: With ajvar (roasted pepper relish) on the side and yogurt to drink.

recipes.title: Cou-Cou
recipes.summary: A smooth, firm cornmeal and okra "pudding" stirred until it holds its shape, traditionally served with flying fish in a spicy Bajan sauce.

items.note: fine yellow cornmeal, mixed with 250 ml cold water
items.name: cornmeal

steps.text: Boil the okra in the salted water until tender.
Lift out the okra with a slotted spoon and keep about half the water in the pot.
Stir the soaked cornmeal into the simmering water and return the okra. Stir constantly with a flat wooden spoon (a cou-cou stick), adding okra water a little at a time.
Keep stirring and turning over low heat until the mixture is smooth and stiff and pulls away from the pot.
Stir in the butter, then shape in a buttered bowl and turn out.

recipes.serving: With steamed flying fish in a tomato, onion and pepper sauce — Barbados's national dish.

recipes.title: Begun Bhorta
recipes.summary: Fire-charred eggplant mashed with pungent mustard oil, raw onion, green chili and cilantro — a smoky Bengali side for rice.

steps.text: Rub the eggplants with a little mustard oil and char them directly over a gas flame, on a grill or under a hot broiler, turning, until the skin is black and the flesh has collapsed.
Let them cool slightly, then peel off the skin and discard the stem. Mash the flesh with a fork or your hand.
Mash in the remaining mustard oil, onion, chili, garlic, cilantro and salt. Taste — it should be smoky, sharp and salty.

tips: Raw mustard oil is the defining flavour; there is no real substitute.
recipes.serving: Hot rice, dal and a selection of other bhortas (mashes) — a classic Bengali lunch.

recipes.title: Booyah
recipes.summary: Booyah is a stew created in Northeastern Wisconsin by Walloon-Belgian immigrants (particularly in the Green Bay area).

steps.text: Place chicken in a large pot and cover with water. Simmer until chicken is well done.
Remove chicken from broth and skim off fat.
Add remaining ingredients to broth.
Remove chicken meat from bones and skin. Cut meat into small pieces and add to broth. Add salt and water to taste.
Cover and let simmer for at least 3 hours. It tastes best when cooked all day.

recipes.title: Carbonade Flamande
recipes.summary: Beef slowly braised in dark Belgian beer with caramelised onions, thickened with a slice of mustard-spread bread.

steps.text: Season the beef and brown it well in batches in the butter. Set aside.
Cook the onions in the same pot until soft and golden (15 minutes). Stir in the flour.
Return the beef, add the beer, stock, sugar, vinegar, thyme and bay, and bring to a simmer.
Spread the bread with mustard and lay it on top, mustard side down.
Cover and braise very gently, stirring occasionally, until the beef is tender and the bread has melted into the sauce.
Season to taste.

recipes.serving: With Belgian fries and mayonnaise.

recipes.title: Riz Gras
alternate_names: Burkinabè rice with meat and vegetables
recipes.summary: Rice cooked in a rich tomato and meat stock with carrots, cabbage and eggplant — a festive dish across Burkina Faso.

steps.text: Brown the meat in the oil. Add the onions and garlic and cook until soft, then the paste and tomatoes for 5 minutes.
Add the water, bouillon and salt and simmer until the meat is nearly tender.
Add the vegetables and Scotch bonnet and simmer until just tender. Lift them out with the meat and keep warm.
Measure about 900 ml of the sauce back into the pot, add the rice, cover tightly and cook on low until tender.
Serve the rice topped with the meat and vegetables.

recipes.title: Shopska Salad
recipes.summary: Tomatoes, cucumber, peppers and onion under a snowy blanket of finely grated white brined cheese.

steps.text: Combine the vegetables and parsley, dress with oil, vinegar and salt, and toss.
Pile into a bowl and grate the cheese thickly over the top so it covers the salad.

recipes.serving: With a glass of rakia, as a starter.
recipes.culture: Created in the 1950s for Bulgaria's tourism board; its white, green and red echo the Bulgarian flag.

recipes.title: Chicken Machboos
recipes.summary: Bahrain's national dish — chicken and basmati rice cooked with dried lime, warm spices, saffron and a breath of rose water.

steps.text: Rinse and soak the rice.
Fry the onions in the ghee until golden, then add garlic, ginger and chilies.
Add the chicken and brown, then the tomatoes, dried limes and all the spices. Fry 2 minutes.
Add the water and salt and simmer, covered, until the chicken is cooked. Lift out the chicken (brown it under the grill if you like).
Measure about 800 ml of broth into the pot, add the drained rice, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on low until tender.
Drizzle the saffron water and rose water over the rice, cover and rest 5 minutes. Serve topped with the chicken and cilantro.

recipes.serving: With daqqus (tomato sauce) and salad.

changes: use vegetable oil instead of ghee

recipes.title: Ibiharage
recipes.summary: Tender red beans fried with onion, garlic and chili until lightly crisp — an everyday Burundian staple.

items.note: 400 g cans, drained — or 250 g dried, soaked and boiled
items.name: canned red kidney beans

steps.text: Fry the onion in the oil until golden, then add the garlic and chili for 1 minute.
Add the beans and salt and fry over medium-high heat, stirring occasionally, until the beans are hot and some have crisped.

recipes.serving: With boiled green bananas, plantain, rice or ugali.

recipes.title: Amiwo
recipes.summary: Cornmeal cooked in a spicy tomato and chicken broth into a smooth, red paste, served with the chicken — a Beninese celebration dish.

steps.text: Simmer the chicken in the water with the chopped onion, garlic, ginger and salt until cooked. Lift out the chicken and keep the broth.
Fry the chicken pieces in the oil until golden; set aside. In the same oil fry the blended onion, tomato paste, tomatoes and chili until thick and darkened (10 minutes).
Add 1 litre of the broth and bring to a boil.
Gradually whisk in the cornmeal, then switch to a wooden spoon and stir hard over low heat until smooth, thick and pulling from the sides (about 10 minutes).
Serve the red paste with the chicken and a little extra sauce.

recipes.title: Nasi Katok
recipes.summary: Brunei's favourite cheap meal — plain rice with crisp turmeric fried chicken and a sweet-hot sambal.

steps.text: Rub the chicken with turmeric, garlic and salt and marinate.
Blend the chilies, shallots, garlic and shrimp paste. Fry in the oil until darkened, add tamarind, sugar and salt and cook to a thick sambal.
Toss the chicken in cornstarch and deep-fry at 170 °C until golden and cooked through (12–15 minutes).
Serve each portion of rice with chicken and a spoonful of sambal.

recipes.culture: "Katok" means "knock" in Malay — from the late-night customers who knocked on the cook's door for a meal.

recipes.title: Sopa de Maní
recipes.summary: A creamy soup of blended raw peanuts, beef, potatoes and vegetables, topped with crisp shoestring fries and parsley.

steps.text: Simmer the beef in 2 litres of the water, skimming, until tender.
Blend the peanuts with the remaining 500 ml water until completely smooth.
Fry the onion, garlic, carrot and pepper in the oil until soft, add cumin and oregano, and add to the broth.
Pour in the peanut milk and simmer, stirring often (it catches easily), with the potatoes, peas and pasta until everything is tender.
Meanwhile fry the potato matchsticks until crisp.
Season the soup and serve topped with fries and parsley.

recipes.title: Moqueca Baiana
recipes.summary: Fish stewed in coconut milk with tomatoes, peppers and red dendê palm oil — the signature dish of Bahia.
equipment: heavy pot — traditionally a clay pan

items.note: firm fish such as snapper or halibut
items.name: firm white fish

steps.text: Season the fish with lime juice, garlic and salt and marinate.
In the pot, layer half the onion, peppers, tomato and cilantro. Lay the fish on top, then cover with the remaining vegetables and most of the cilantro.
Pour over the coconut milk and dendê, and add the chili.
Cover and simmer gently without stirring — shake the pan instead — until the fish flakes.
Taste for salt and scatter with the remaining cilantro.

recipes.serving: With white rice, farofa de dendê (toasted cassava flour) and pirão (a fish-broth porridge).
recipes.culture: Afro-Brazilian cuisine in Bahia is built on dendê palm oil, brought by enslaved West Africans along with many of the region's culinary traditions.

recipes.title: Peas 'n' Rice
recipes.summary: Rice cooked with pigeon peas, salt pork or bacon, tomato paste and thyme — the side dish on every Bahamian table.

steps.text: Fry the bacon until it renders, then add the onion, pepper and celery and cook until soft.
Stir in the tomato paste and thyme for 1 minute, then add the peas with their liquid, the water, salt and pepper and bring to a boil.
Stir in the rice, cover tightly and cook on low until tender.

recipes.title: Ema Datshi
recipes.summary: Bhutan's national dish — green chilies simmered with onion and tomato in a melting, tangy cheese sauce.

items.note: long green chilies; use milder ones unless you love heat
items.name: fresh green chili

items.note: Bhutanese datshi is a soft cow's-milk cheese; feta mixed with farmer's cheese is a common substitute
items.name: feta

steps.text: Simmer the chilies, onion, garlic and oil in the water.
Add the tomato and cheese and simmer, stirring gently, until the cheese melts into a sauce (about 5 minutes). Don't boil hard.
Season — the cheese is salty, so taste first.

recipes.serving: With Bhutanese red rice.

recipes.title: Seswaa
recipes.summary: Beef boiled slowly with just salt and onion until it falls apart, then pounded into tender shreds — Botswana's national dish.

items.note: on the bone; brisket or chuck also work
items.name: beef shank

steps.text: Put the beef, onion and salt in a heavy pot, cover with water and simmer, topping up the water, until the meat falls off the bone.
Remove the bones. Let most of the liquid evaporate.
Pound and stir the meat with a wooden spoon until it breaks into fine, tender shreds coated in its own juices. Season.

recipes.serving: With pap (stiff maize porridge) and morogo (wild spinach) or beans.
recipes.culture: Traditionally cooked by men in three-legged iron pots and pounded with a wooden pestle at big gatherings.

recipes.title: Draniki
recipes.summary: Belarus's beloved potato pancakes — grated potato and onion fried until crisp, served hot with sour cream.

steps.text: Grate the onion first and then the potatoes into it — the onion keeps the potatoes from browning. Drain off some of the liquid.
Mix in the egg, flour, salt and pepper.
Fry spoonfuls in hot oil, flattening slightly, until golden and crisp on both sides (about 3 minutes per side).
Serve hot with sour cream.

recipes.serving: Also with machanka (pork and sour-cream gravy) or mushrooms.

recipes.title: Belizean Stew Chicken
recipes.summary: Chicken marinated in red recado, browned in caramelised sugar and simmered with onion and peppers into a dark, savoury stew.

steps.text: Rub the chicken with the annatto, vinegar, garlic, cumin, oregano, pepper and salt. Marinate.
Heat the oil and sugar in a heavy pot until the sugar turns dark amber, then add the chicken and brown it all over.
Add the onion, pepper and celery and cook for 3 minutes.
Add the water, cover and simmer until the chicken is tender and the sauce is rich.

recipes.serving: With rice and beans, potato salad and fried plantain.

recipes.title: Poutine
recipes.summary: Crisp double-fried chips topped with squeaky fresh cheese curds and hot, peppery brown gravy.

steps.text: Soak the potato batons in cold water to remove starch, then dry thoroughly.
For the gravy, melt the butter, stir in the flour and cook, stirring, until nut-brown. Whisk in the stock and pepper and simmer until thick enough to coat a spoon. Keep hot.
Fry the potatoes at 160 °C in batches for 5–6 minutes until soft but pale. Drain.
Raise the oil to 190 °C and fry again for 2–3 minutes until golden and crisp. Drain and salt.
Pile the fries into bowls, scatter over the cheese curds, and pour over the hot gravy so the curds just begin to melt.

tips: Fresh curds should squeak against your teeth — don't refrigerate them before using.
recipes.culture: Born in rural Quebec diners in the late 1950s; the name is Quebec slang for "a mess".

recipes.title: Soft Sugar Cookies

steps.text: In a large bowl, beat eggs lightly to break the yolks as one would for scrambled eggs, then mix in the shortening. If using butter, soften it slightly beforehand by heating it a little. The shortening/egg mixture should be loose.
Mix in the sugar, then add the salt to the liquid mixture.

Add the baking powder, then slowly add the flour as needed to reach a proper doughy state (in essence, able to be shaped without sticking to one's hands too much). You may not need all of the flour, or you may even need a little more based on your eggs and how closely you measured.
Make balls and place onto a greased or parchment-lined pan then into an oven heated to 175°C (350°F), and let bake for between 15–20 minutes.

tips: Feel free to switch out half the sugar with another sweet item, like honey.

Adding some cinnamon and nutmeg gives a good flavor.

steps.text: Boil the potatoes in their skins until just tender at the edges but firm in the centre. Cool and refrigerate overnight.

Heat half the butter and oil in the pan over medium heat. Add the potatoes and press lightly into a thick cake.
Cook without stirring until a golden crust forms underneath, shaking the pan now and then.
Slide the rösti onto a plate, invert another plate on top and flip. Add the rest of the fat to the pan and slide the rösti back in, uncooked side down.

recipes.title: Ndole

recipes.summary: Ndole is a popular traditional soup recipe in Cameroon that is made with the combination of spinach and bitter leaves as well as crayfish, shrimp, and beef. It is also a recipe for ceremony.

steps.text: Season the beef in a big pot with salt, maggi, and one-third of the onions, then boil until the meat is soft.

Grind half the remaining onion and garlic to a paste, then stir into the meat and peanut mixture.

recipes.title: Frijoles Antioqueños
recipes.summary: Antioqueño beans is an icon of Colombian food.

steps.text: Wash beans and let hydrate overnight by covering with twice its volume of water.
The next day, remove any floating beans.
Heat the oil in a pressure cooker. Add scallions and let fry until they start to brown. Add tomato, cumin, broth cube, and allspice. This is called "hogao", a basic sauce for many Colombian dishes.
Add 6 cups water, the beans, and plantain. Bring to a boil over medium heat.
Cover the pressure cooker, and let cook for 30 minutes.
Let cool, then open the pressure cooker.
Check water level, add the meat if using, and cover again. Cook for another 30 minutes.
Taste for salt. If you want a thicker mixture, you can cook uncovered over low heat.

tips: When serving, you can put additional hogao on top.
You can serve with white rice, avocado, ground beef, roasted beef, fried plantain, roasted chicken, corn arepas, and many other combinations.
Trasnochado beans, eaten one day after being cooked, are a great option to eat the beans with a delicious concentrated flavor.

To make bandeja paisa, serve a portion of Antioqueño beans, a portion of white rice, a portion of ground beef, a slice of avocado, one fried chorizo sausage, fried ripe plantain, one fried blood sausage, pork rind, and one fried egg on top of the rice.
Another delicious way to serve these beans is with cazuelitas: serve half of a cazuelita with the beans, and add to it corn, shredded beef (ropa vieja), avocado, and ground pork rind.

recipes.title: Christmas Ham
recipes.summary: The ancient Romans, who sacrificed a pig to their god Saturn about the same time Christmas is celebrated nowadays, are probably the starters of a Christmas tradition still alive in some parts of the world.

steps.text: If ham is frozen, thaw it in its plastic package, for 3 days in the refrigerator for a 7kg ham, 5 days for a 10kg ham.

Before putting the ham in the oven, take it out from the refrigerator and let come closer to room temperature. If you intend to put the ham in the oven in the evening, take it out during the early morning. The ham should be about 10 °C (50 °F) when you put it in the oven.
Use a wet paper towel to clean the ham a bit; then dry it.

Place ham on baking tray in oven, with some water on the tray. Or, if you have a large roasting bag, there is no need for water. Do not use only the oven rack, as nothing will catch all the liquid from the ham if the roasting bag fails, messing up your oven. However, you can put the ham on the rack if you put a baking tray beneath that to catch drips. Aluminum foil can be used on the baking tray to protect it.
Preheat oven to 200 °C (390 °F) and let ham roast in the oven for half an hour. You can skip this if you are not worried about the possible bacteria on the ham.

Turn temperature down, and cook at 100–125 °C (210–260 °F), for about 1 hour/kg (a 7 kg ham will take 7 hours or more) until a meat thermometer in the center of the ham reads 75–80 °C (158–176 °F). Traditional ham is ready at 80 °C but most take the ham out of the oven at 77 °C or so, when the ham has more water left in it and is considered tastier.
After you take the ham out of the oven, wait a little while before removing the thermometer. It is recommended you do not pour the liquid from the bag or baking tray down the drain.

Wait until ham is cool enough to handle, then glaze it all over with mustard and breadcrumbs. First remove the rind from the ham, then cover the ham with mustard, then with breadcrumbs. Bake in a 250 °C (480 °F) oven for 10 minutes.
The ham is ready to eat when it has cooled down a bit. This makes about enough for 3 or 4 people for a week, but if you think you will not eat it all within a week, freeze the rest.

tips: A 10 kg ham is considered better-tasting as the pig has gotten bigger.

The use of a meat thermometer is recommended because the actual temperature of an oven commonly varies from its setting; thus the ham can be severely under- or overcooked if you do not use a thermometer. The thermometer should be placed in the middle of the ham. Be careful that it does not touch the oven walls. You can test if the thermometer works properly before using it by dipping it in boiling water–it should show about 100 °C (212 °F).

It is possible to salt a ham yourself if you buy ham from a farm or butcher or buy a pig in time to fatten it for Christmas. There are several methods available; here is one that is called tönkkösuolaus: Dissolve 1.8 kg large crystal salt into 10 L water, and cool to 0 °C or slightly lower. Fully submerge a 10 kg ham in the brine, and let it brine at around 0 °C for 2 months, replacing the brine from time to time. During the last week you can keep ham in water only if you want it to be slightly less salty.

Several people swear by sauna-cooked ham, in which case you will put the ham in a sauna instead of an oven (glazing still done in oven). It will take maybe 12–24 hours for a ham in a 100 °C sauna, and several days in a 80 °C sauna. Use a meat thermometer if you use a sauna to cook a ham and remember to have something beneath the ham collecting all the liquid. Often people also use a wood-burning stove to cook a ham, this method is hardest as you can not use a meat thermometer easily with one, so unless you have good instructions to the very oven you have (or have a spare ham just in case), this would not be recommended for first-time Christmas ham lovers.

recipes.title: French Omelette
recipes.summary: A French omelette is a dish consisting of fried beaten eggs, often with an added filling. The center of the omelette should be just barely cooked, and a little runny. The outside should be cooked, but not browned (or only slightly browned).

steps.text: Loosely beat the eggs. Season the mixture with some salt and pepper.
Heat a frying pan. Add oil and a small amount of butter when the pan starts to get hot. Enough to coat the pan entirely, but no more. Remove any excess oil.
Let the pan get as hot as you can, without burning the butter, and keep the flame high.
Pour the egg mixture into the pan and quickly tilt the pan to let it spread around the bottom.

With a spoon or spatula, pull the solidified edges towards the center and tilt the pan to let the egg mixture fill the gap again. Keep repeating this (quickly) until there's not enough liquid egg left to fill the gap. The top of the omelette should still be liquid.

Turn the heat down a little lower to fold the egg. Use a spatula to pry the edges loose from the pan. When the omelette is completely loose from the pan. Fold one part over the other. You can fold half of the omelette over the other half, or fold one third of the omelette inwards and then fold the remaining flap over that, to create a thicker, less wide omelette.
Slide the omelette onto the plate.

tips: The center of a good omelette should just be a little runny. When serving omelettes to children, pregnant women, or elderly or ill people, give the omelette a little more time to cook.
To decrease the amount of eggs used, use fewer eggs, and add some milk.

Omelettes are often cooked with extra ingredients, or a 'filling'. How ingredients should be added depends on the ingredient. Some ingredients, like cheese, can be added to the egg mixture. Some should be fried before making the omelette (possibly in the same pan as the omelette, before adding the eggs). To use the ingredients more as a filling, than as a part of the mixture, add them to the omelette just before folding. There are many ingredients and fillings that can be used in omelettes. Some suggestions include:
Cooked bacon.
Any kind of cheese.
Broccoli.
Olives.
Chopped tomatoes, optionally with seeds removed
Ham, salami, or prosciutto.
Sautéed Mushrooms.

recipes.title: Bangers and Mash
recipes.summary: You can fry or grill sausages quickly, but in this recipe they are cooked slowly (as recommended by Nigel Slater, no less) so as to really bring out the flavour. Some people like baked beans with their sausage and mash, some people like gravy, and some people don't need either.

steps.text: Put a large heavy frying pan on a hob over a medium heat. Put in a little vegetable oil (if desired) and let it warm up.
Then place the sausages in a single layer in the frying pan. Let them fry a minute or so, then turn them over, fry another minute, turn them around again, to try and get a bit of colour all over.

Once they've been in the hot pan for 5 minutes or so, turn the heat right down to low. Let them fry very gently for the next 25 minutes, turning them over every 5 or 10 minutes so they get cooked evenly. You can cook them for longer than this (even up to about an hour on a very low heat). Always make sure the sausages are cooked all the way through (no pinkness should remain).
Peel the potatoes and chop them roughly into pieces around 1 or 2 cm thick. Add them to a large pan of boiling water and boil vigorously for 15 minutes.

Add a generous knob of butter and a splash of milk to the potatoes, and mash them all up with a potato masher.

tips: You do not need to prick the sausages—that only lets tasty juices escape! Similarly you don't necessarily need to separate them one from another until after they've cooked.

recipes.title: Irish Soda Bread

steps.text: Preheat oven to 325°F (160°C).
Grease and flour a 9x5-inch loaf pan.
Combine flour, baking powder, baking soda, sugar, and salt in a large mixing bowl.
Blend egg and buttermilk together, and add all at once to the flour mixture.
Mix until just moistened. Too much mixing will make it tough.
Stir in butter; pour into prepared pan.
Bake for 65–70 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted in the bread comes out clean. The loaf should sound hollow if you tap the base.

recipes.title: Basic Indian Tomato Gravy
recipes.summary: This traditional Indian tomato gravy can be used as a base for all sorts of vegetables, boiled eggs, cubed paneer or chicken. This is often referred to as a "curry". It is usually eaten with plain white rice or rice mixtures.

steps.text: Fry the onions in hot ghee until they start to brown.
Add the ginger and garlic and stir, then add the powdered spices. Blend well.
Throw in the tomatoes and salt to taste.
Turn the flame down to medium and cover for ten minutes. This will form a spicy gravy to which you can add any mixture of vegetables or boiled eggs or fried fish or chicken or lamb/goat.

tips: If adding cooked vegetables, keep the pot on the flame until they are uniformly heated; for uncooked vegetables, cook as long as necessary.

With chicken/lamb/goat, add the marinated poultry/meat after frying the ginger garlic paste and adding the dry spice powders. Sear the poultry/meat on high heat, turning the pieces continuously for about 10–15 minutes until the juices get sealed inside. Add the tomatoes after this step. Continue cooking as per above recipe. Alternatively, you have the option of frying /roasting/grilling the marinated poultry/meat separately, before adding to the curry, then letting it simmer for at least 20 minutes.
You can add a little cayenne and cumin and leave out the chili powder (though "chili powder" in Indian recipes is cayenne/powdered chilis)
Depending on the freshness of your spices, you may want to add extra spices in the same ratio to achieve a stronger flavour.

Generally, in Indian cuisine, for lamb or goat (known locally as 'mutton'), you can use all the above ingredients to make the gravy (curry). Some recipes use curd/yogurt, while some use tomatoes for the balancing tart flavour. With chicken, lamb and goat, marination is preferred. Also, various spice powders and spices (sabut garam masala) are added depending on the recipe. For example, cloves and cinnamon can be added to the hot oil, to give an excellent flavour.
For a vegan version of this recipe, substitute the ghee with coconut oil or other vegetable oil.

You can also use a pressure cooker instead of the stovetop; in this case, cook it for 6−7 whistles on a medium flame. This is especially useful when cooking lamb or goat as the meat is tougher than chicken.
You can also use fried onions as garnish to get a gravy with a different flavor. This is used frequently in chicken recipes.

recipes.title: Chicken Vindaloo
recipes.summary: Vindaloo is a hot and spicy dish from the Goa region of India. Its heavy use of vinegar and the traditional meat of pork are due to the Portuguese influence on the area.

steps.text: Take a thick-based frying pan, and pour into it enough vegetable oil to cover the base, with a little excess. Heat on a stovetop.
Slice the onions into fairly thin slivers. When the oil is very hot, add the onions.
Turn the stove down to a low heat, so the onions just gently sauté. After around 3 minutes they should be starting to caramelize.
Gradually turn up the heat and keep stirring the onions. You want them to brown quite heavily without burning.
Add the white wine vinegar, it will sizzle, and after a while will evaporate. Keep stirring. Fry for several more minutes, until they are very brown, but not burnt.
Remove the onions from the pan into a bowl, taking care to let as much oil as possible drip back into the pan. You should now have a bowl of nicely crisped fried onions.

Add the onions to a blender or food processor. Add around 1 tablespoon of oil, and process for around a minute until you have a fairly thick, dark brown sauce. This is the basic onion sauce from which vindaloo is made. It's also the onion sauce that gives the vindaloo the majority of its 'hot' taste, as it builds up as you eat the dish.
Remove sauce from blender and set aside.
Coarsely chop the garlic cloves (and ginger if you're using it). De-seed the chili peppers and chop in the same way. Add the chopped garlic and chillies to the food processor.

Blend the garlic and chillies until you have a fairly grainy (but liquid) sauce. For this I used an attachment on my blender which is intended to grind coffee beans. It has a much smaller container and so there's less waste.
Add the turmeric, coriander powder, garam masala and cinnamon to the sauce. Stir it until it's well mixed, and set aside.
Gently crush the black peppercorns in a mortar and pestle. Once coarse, add the mustard seed and rock salt. Continue blending until all the spices form a nice coarse powder.
Pour a little oil into a saucepan. Add the spiced garlic and chili paste to the pan. It needs to be slightly floating on oil, not touching the bottom of the pan.
When the sauce is quite hot and bubbling, add the chopped meat. Keep stirring so the meat absorbs the spice mix, until it is browned and mostly cooked.

Now add the onion sauce to the pan. After stirring for 1 minute, add a little water and stir for another 2 minutes, then turn the heat to quite low. The sauce at this stage should be quite runny, and orange/tan in color. Remember a lot is going to evaporate off as it cooks.
At this stage you can add some vegetables. Half a cup of frozen peas works well.
Place a lid over the pan, and cook for around 30-40 minutes. Keep checking and stirring the pan every 5 or 10 minutes to make sure it doesn't stick or burn.The sauce will darken in color as it cooks.
Towards the last 15 minutes of cooking time, boil 2 cups of pilau, or basmati rice in a pan.
To serve- spoon the curry over the top of the rice. Sprinkle the chopped coriander leaves over the curry, and serve immediately.

tips: Powdered or dried ingredients can be substituted for fresh, but at the expense of taste.
If you don't have fresh ginger use 2 cloves garlic + 1 tsp dried ginger powder.
Double the amount of each of these ingredients:
chosen chilies (if you like very spicy curry)

garam masala (if you like very spicy curry)

recipes.title: Ghevar
recipes.summary: Ghevar is an Indian delicacy originally from the state of Rajasthan. It is made with a round mold and has a crispy but porous texture. The following recipe has been entered with inputs from Tarla Dalal recipe book.

steps.text: Combine the sugar and water in a saucepan. Simmer until it reaches a 1-string consistency syrup.
Remove from the heat and keep warm.
Combine the flour, arrowroot, and melted ghee in a bowl.
Very gradually add 1 cup of water in a thin stream, whisking continuously and taking care to see that an emulsion is formed and the water and ghee do not separate.

Add 2 more cups of water again in a thin stream while whisking continuously. At no point should the ghee and water separate. The batter should be of a very thin coating consistency, a little thinner than crêpe batter. More water can be added if required to achieve the required consistency. Keep the batter in a cool place away from the heat.
Add melted ghee to a kadhai or other pot/pan. If desired, place a ghevar mould or other metal ring mould in the pan. The ghee should come up to ¾ of the height of the mould.

Heat the pan over medium heat, and gradually pour a ladleful of the batter directly into the centre of the mould in a very thin stream. The batter should froth and migrate towards the edges of the mold.

When the froth subsides, gradually add another spoonful to the centre in a thin stream. If the batter builds up in the center, use a skewer to push it towards the edges and maintain a hole in the center. Repeat seven times, adding the batter to the centre hole each time.
Increase the heat, and pour a few ladlefuls of hot ghee into the centre to help the ghevar cook.

When the centre is firm and cooked and the whole thing is golden brown, pull the ghevar out gently by inserting a wooden skewer in the centre and pulling it out of the ghee. Let any excess ghee drip off.
Immerse ghevar in sugar syrup, drain quickly, and place on a serving plate.
Repeat the cooking steps, using the remaining batter to make 9 pieces of ghevar.

tips: A mould is not required to cook the ghevar; if the pot containing the ghee has a small enough diameter, it will act as the mold to shape the ghevar.
Usually ghevar is served with piping hot rabri, a variety of very thick sweetened milk.

recipes.title: Indian Hard Tack
recipes.summary: Baati is a hard, unleavened bread cooked in desert areas of Rajasthan, Malwa, and Gujarat in North India. It is prized there for its exceptionally long life and high energy content, as well as the minimal quantity of water required in its preparation.

Soften the onion in the butter, stir in the flour and cook 1 minute, then whisk in the milk and simmer until thick.
Roughly chop the potatoes and fold them and the fish into the sauce. Season generously with pepper — it should be chunky, not smooth.

recipes.serving: With dark, sweet rye bread (rúgbrauð) and butter.

steps.text: Either pour espresso over gelato and serve, or serve them side by side for diner to mix at the table.

recipes.summary: Agnolotti in brodo is a very simple and delicious Italian pasta soup containing agnolotti, small ravioli filled most commonly with meat. This soup is delicious on a cold day when you haven't much time to devote to preparing a tasty meal.

steps.text: Bring the chicken broth to a rolling boil. If using water and chicken stock cubes, bring the water to a boil, add the stock cubes and let dissolve.
Add the agnolotti and cook according to the instructions on the package.
Add the cream, freshly-ground black pepper, and chopped parsley about 2 minutes before the end of the cooking, and turn down the heat.
Add the dash of sherry just before serving. If serving to children, dish out their portions first, then add the sherry for the grown-ups.
Let stand for a few minutes to marry the flavors, then serve, sprinkled with grated Parmesan cheese and enjoy.

recipes.title: American Marinara Sauce
recipes.summary: This is the classic expensive restaurant edition. You only live once.

steps.text: Heat a large pot over medium heat until hot (approximately 5 minutes).
Add butter and oil; heat until clear and the bubbling stops.
Add onion; gently sauté for 1 minute.
Reduce heat to medium-low.
Add garlic; gently sauté for 1 minute.
Add tomato juice.
Add tomatoes, one at a time, crushing completely using your hands (watch for spurts).
Add oregano and red pepper flakes. Stir to combine.
Cover and reduce heat to low. Simmer for 10–15 minutes.
Add 1 tsp salt and sugar, black pepper, and tomato paste; Stir until paste is incorporated.
Cover and simmer for 10 minutes

Taste and season accordingly. You do not want the sauce to be salty, just not unsalty. You do not want the sauce to be sweet, just not sour. Season by adding the remaining salt and sugar a little at a time, stirring completely between tastes.
Serve over al dente spaghetti with a side of Italian sausage or meatballs and a deep sweet red wine; serves 4, make this for two and enjoy again tomorrow night!

recipes.title: Cacio e Pepe
recipes.summary: Roman pasta with only three ingredients — pecorino, black pepper and starchy pasta water whipped into a creamy sauce.

items.note: for the pasta water — use less than usual, the cheese is salty
items.name: salt

steps.text: Cook the pasta in a smaller amount of water than usual (about 2 litres) so it gets very starchy. Lightly salt it.
Toast the pepper in a large dry frying pan for 1 minute, then add a ladle of pasta water and let it simmer.
In a bowl, mash the pecorino with a few spoonfuls of lukewarm (not hot) pasta water into a thick, smooth paste.
Two minutes before the pasta is al dente, transfer it to the pepper pan with tongs and finish cooking it there, adding pasta water as needed.
Take the pan off the heat and let it cool for 30 seconds. Add the cheese paste and toss vigorously, adding splashes of water until the sauce is creamy and coats the pasta. Serve immediately.

tips: If the pan is too hot the cheese turns into clumps; off the heat and lukewarm water are the keys.
recipes.culture: A dish of Roman shepherds, who carried dried pasta, aged pecorino and pepper because none of them spoil.

recipes.title: Caponata
recipes.summary: Caponata is a Sicilian eggplant dish consisting of cooked vegetables with chopped up fried eggplant, celery, sweetened vinegar, and capers with sweet sauce.

steps.text: Strip the filaments from the celery sticks and blanch in lightly salted water for five minutes. Drain and cut the celery into bite-size pieces, sauté them in a little oil, and set aside.
Wash and dice the eggplant, strain, and sprinkle liberally with salt, and let sit for several hours to draw out the bitterness. In the meantime, blanch, peel, seed and chop the tomatoes.

Once the eggplant has sat, rinse away the salt and pat the pieces dry. Finely slice the onion and sauté them in olive oil; once they have turned translucent, add the capers, pine nuts, olives, and tomatoes. Continue cooking, stirring with a wooden spoon, until the tomatoes are done, about 15 minutes, and then remove the pot from the heat.

While the tomatoes are cooking, heat another pan of oil and fry the eggplant, in batches, to prevent lowering of the frying temperature. When the last batch is done, return the tomato pot to the heat and stir in the eggplant together with the previously sautéed celery. Cook for several minutes over low flame, stirring gently, then stir in the vinegar and the sugar; when the vinegar has almost completely evaporated, remove the pot from the fire and let it cool.
Serve the caponata cold with a garnish of fresh basil. Caponata keeps for several days in the refrigerator.

tips: You can serve this on toast as an appetizer, as a side dish, or as a main dish for a light meal.

recipes.title: Fresh Mozzarella Bruschetta
recipes.summary: Bruschette are small, open-faced sandwiches of tomato and mozzarella cheese. They are delicious, quick and easy to make, and perfect appetizers.

steps.text: Cut bread into ½ inch (1.27 cm) slices on the diagonal.
Lightly toast bread in the oven on both sides.
Cut tomatoes into ¼ inch (0.75 cm) slices, and place one on each slice of bread.
Cut mozzarella balls into ¼ inch (0.75cm) slices and place on top of tomato.
Slice basil into thin strips and sprinkle on top with the oregano.
Combine olive oil and balsamic vinegar (to taste) in a small bowl
Drizzle bruschetta with the mixture and sprinkle with salt and pepper.

tips: An optional re-toasting with toppings on will make the mozzarella melt and be even more delicious.
Authentic Italian bruschetta begins with rubbing roasted garlic cloves on the toasted bread slices.

recipes.title: Lady Finger Cookies
recipes.summary: Savoiardi are a sponge-like cookie originally from the Aosta Valley of Italy in the Alps, once known as the Duchy of Savoy (whence its name is derived). They figure prominently in several desserts, including puddings and tiramisu, as they absorb liquids excellently.

steps.text: Whip the eggs until very thick. Add sugar, oil, vanilla, baking powder, and lemon juice, and stir until combined.
Slowly fold in flour with a wooden spoon, continually adding until you have a very thick batter (you may need more or less flour).
On a large flat surface, such as a cutting board or plate, sift the powdered sugar.
Using a teaspoon, scoop walnut-sized balls of batter onto the powdered sugar, and roll each into an oval.
Transfer cookies to a cookie sheet lined with parchment paper, and cover with a single layer of parchment.
Place pans into an oven preheated to 200°C (392°F).
Bake for 5–15 minutes, until biscotti begin to turn golden.
Cool completely.

tips: If you choose to buy savoiardi in a store rather than make them, be sure of the date they were made as they have a very short shelf life.
Properly made savoiardi should never be soft.
Savoiardi are often enjoyed dipped in brandy and espresso coffee.

recipes.summary: Marinara (mariner's) sauce is a southern Italian tomato sauce usually made with tomatoes, garlic, herbs (such as basil), and onion. However, there are many variations. Some of these include the addition of capers, olives and spices.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a saucepan over medium heat until it shimmers.
Add the onions and garlic, and sauté them for about 2 minutes until the onions are translucent.
Add the thyme, basil and bell pepper. Cook 5 minutes more.
Add the tomatoes and sugar. Bring to a boil and then lower to a light simmer, stirring occasionally for 30 minutes.
Season with salt to taste.
Serve hot by ladling over pasta, seafood or rice.

recipes.title: Ricotta Lasagne
recipes.summary: Lasagne is a baked pasta dish.

steps.text: Remove sausage casings, and break sausage into small bits.
Sauté sausage and ground beef in 5-quart (4.7 L) saucepan or Dutch oven over medium heat with onion and garlic until the meat is browned.
Add sugar, 1 tablespoon salt, basil, fennel, pepper, and half the parsley; mix well.
Add tomatoes, tomato paste and water, mashing the tomatoes a bit. Bring the sauce to a boil then reduce heat and simmer, covered and stirring occasionally for 1½ hours.
Preheat oven to .
Cook and drain pasta.
In a medium bowl mix ricotta, egg, ½ teaspoon salt and remaining parsley.
Assemble your lasagna in a inch roasting pan (listed bottom to top):
Bottom layer of sauce (approx. 1½ cups / 375 g / 13.2 oz)
Layer of pasta (overlapping slightly)
Layer of ½ the ricotta mixture
Layer of ⅓ of the mozzarella
Sauce layer (again, about 1½ cups / 375 g / 13.2 oz)

Layer of pasta

Layer of remaining sauce

Layer of remaining mozzarella
Cover the lasagna with foil and bake 30 minutes covered, then 25 minutes uncovered (or until bubbly and lightly browned). Cool for at least 20 minutes before serving.

tips: Uncooked lasagnas freeze very well so the extra work can be done well in advance. You can make several batches at a time and freeze the extras to thaw out and cook later.

recipes.title: Tagliatelle Bake
recipes.summary: This recipe for tagliatelle bake is a typical dish prepared traditionally in the South of Italy on Sundays as a way to serve a rich course without spending too much time in the kitchen.

steps.text: Preheat the oven to 180°C (160°C convection / 350°F / gas mark 4).
Heat 3 tbsp oil in a large pan. Add the onion, carrot and celery. Cook gently until soft but not coloured.
Add the minced beef and cook until browned, breaking up the mince as much as possible.
Add the parsley. Pour in the white wine and cook for 5 minutes to burn off the alcohol.
Season to taste and add the chopped tomatoes. Cook over a low heat for 30 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Bring a large pan of water to the boil and salt it. Add the pasta and cook following pack instructions or until the pasta is firm to the bite (al dente). Drain the pasta.

Grease an oven dish and thinly cover the bottom with some of the tomato sauce. Fill with half the quantity of the pasta, the diced mozzarella, half of the tomato sauce, half of the cream and cover with half of the grated Parmesan cheese.
Fill the oven dish with another layer of tagliatelle, the remaining mozzarella, the tomato sauce, the cream and cover with Parmesan cheese and some freshly grated nutmeg.
Bake in the oven for about 30 minutes or until the top of the dish is golden. Remove from the oven and leave to cool for a few minutes.
Add a few basil leaves and serve.

recipes.summary: Jamaican banana fritters are a traditional dessert and snack dish in the Caribbean. They can be served by themselves, in a platter along with other fritters, or with different toppings, like cinnamon, coconut, or even ice cream.

steps.text: Peel the bananas and mash them in a bowl until runny.
Heat oil in a deep frying pan at medium heat.
Add the sugar, milk, vanilla, salt, and flour to the bananas and mix until approximately the consistency of pancake batter or a bit thinner.
Drop tablespoons of the mixture into the heated oil, and fry until edges are firm, then flip to cook other side until golden brown.
Drain on a towel and serve hot.

tips: Sprinkling sugar, nutmeg, cinnamon or coconut on the fritters after frying.
Serving with a scoop of ice cream.

recipes.title: Rice and Peas
recipes.summary: Rice cooked with kidney beans in coconut milk, fragrant with thyme, scallion, allspice and a whole Scotch bonnet.

items.note: whole and unbroken — for aroma, not heat
items.name: Scotch bonnet chili

steps.text: Bring the beans with their liquid, coconut milk, water, garlic, scallion, thyme, allspice, Scotch bonnet and salt to a boil.
Stir in the rice. The liquid should cover the rice by about 1.5 cm; add water if needed.
Cover tightly and cook on low heat until the rice is tender and the liquid absorbed.
Remove the scallion, thyme and the whole pepper (carefully — don't burst it). Fluff and serve.

tips: In Jamaica "peas" means kidney beans; pigeon peas (gungo peas) are used at Christmas.
recipes.serving: With curry goat, brown stew chicken or jerk chicken.

recipes.title: Galayet Bandora
recipes.summary: Ripe tomatoes fried down in olive oil with garlic and hot green chili until jammy — a quick, rustic dish scooped up with bread.

steps.text: Fry the onion (if using), garlic and chili in the olive oil until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes, salt and pepper and cook over medium-high heat, stirring, until the tomatoes collapse into a thick, glossy stew.
Top with pine nuts and a drizzle of olive oil.

recipes.serving: From the pan, with warm flatbread and olives.

recipes.title: Beef Yakiniku Pizza
recipes.summary: Yakiniku is a Japanese term referring broadly to grilled or barbecued meat dishes. This recipe tops pizza dough with a yakiniku-style beef stir-fry.

items.prep: cut into 2 x 1 x 1 cm pieces
items.name: beef

steps.text: Combine flours, yeast, sugar, water, and salt to make a dough.
Cover with plastic wrap, and rest the dough 10 minutes until expanded.
Heat the oil in a non-stick pan. Add the onion and capsicum, and sauté for 10 seconds.
Add the tenderloin and the water. Add the mirin, soy sauce, and oyster sauce.
Add the dissolved cornflour, salt, and sugar. Stir until well-mixed and slightly thickened.
Separate the solids from the extra sauce. Reserve the sauce to serve with the pizza.
Roll out the pizza dough to a 10 cm diameter. Spread the meat topping on top.
Bake pizza in the oven at 220°C for 20 minutes.
Serve hot with the dipping sauces.
